title: Best Time to Buy a TV: A Month-by-Month Guide
dek: TV prices follow the same calendar every year. Here is when each kind of buyer should shop, what to check before paying, and where the advice comes from.
author: viewdeals-desk
meta_description: When TVs are cheapest: Black Friday, the weeks before the Super Bowl and spring closeouts. A month-by-month guide with sources and a buying checklist.

sections.heading: The short answer
paragraphs: There are three good windows a year, and which one is best depends on what you want. If you want the lowest price on a mainstream set, shop in late November or in the weeks before the Super Bowl. If you want last year's high-end model at a markdown, shop in spring, once its replacement is in stores. If you want this year's newest model, expect to pay the most in spring and less with every month you wait.

That pattern is not our invention. NerdWallet's guide, updated in January 2026, names Super Bowl season, spring, Prime Day and Black Friday as the times to buy, and DealNews, which counts the deals it lists each month, calls Black Friday the best time of the year. We explain each window below and say where each claim comes from.

sections.heading: Why TV prices move on a calendar
paragraphs: TV makers work to a yearly cycle. New models are usually announced at the CES trade show in January, according to DealNews, and they start reaching stores in March or April, according to Jim Willcox of Consumer Reports, quoted by NerdWallet. A new TV costs the most on the day it arrives and gets cheaper as the year goes on.

Two things follow from that. By February, the current models have been on sale for close to a year, so their prices have already come down. And once the new sets arrive in spring, stores need the shelf space, so the outgoing models are cleared out. NerdWallet's sources say those closeouts can run into the summer.

sections.heading: Black Friday: the lowest prices, with one catch
paragraphs: Black Friday is the window both sources rank first for price. DealNews bases that on its own listings: in the years it reports, it found more TV deals in Black Friday week than in the weeks around it, and a larger share of them were deals its editors rated as the best. NerdWallet adds the reason: so many stores compete at once that they change prices during the day to match each other. Both note that the sales now begin in October, so there is no need to wait for the Friday itself.

The catch is the special model. Some makers build TVs just for Black Friday. Consumer Reports' Willcox, quoted by NerdWallet, calls these derivatives: they look like a current model but can be missing features. The test is simple. Search for the exact model number. If no other store sells it and nobody has reviewed it, treat it as a derivative and compare it with a model you can read about.

sections.heading: The Super Bowl window
paragraphs: The weeks before the Super Bowl are the second good window. Football sales start in January and run to the game in February, and they lean towards large screens. DealNews is a little cooler on it than NerdWallet: it says prices have not quite fallen back to their Black Friday lows by then, but that strong deals still appear, especially on big sets. If you missed November, this is the next chance, and you are buying a model that has had a year of reviews.

sections.heading: Spring and summer: last year's best sets
paragraphs: Spring is when the trade-off is clearest. The newly arrived models are at their most expensive, and the ones they replace are being cleared. In our view the older set is often the better buy for someone who does not need the newest features. DealNews reports more TV deals in February than in January as stores make room, and a steady number in March.

Prime Day, usually in July, is the summer window. NerdWallet describes it as second only to Black Friday, and strongest for mid-range sets, smart TVs and last year's models. Other big stores run their own sales the same week, so compare before buying.

sections.heading: What to check before you buy
paragraphs: Check the model number and the year. A sale price on a two-year-old model is not the same as a sale price on last year's. The model number tells you which you are looking at, and it is how you find reviews.
Check who is selling it. On a marketplace listing, the seller may not be the store whose name is on the site, and returns can work differently.

Check the price-match and return rules. Some stores refund the difference if the price falls soon after you buy, but NerdWallet notes that items bought during sales such as Black Friday are often excluded. DealNews suggests looking for a window of about two weeks.
Don't pay for features you won't use. DealNews advises skipping 8K for now, and both sources point out that a cheaper set plus a plug-in streaming stick does the same job as built-in smart features.

sections.heading: How we will keep this guide honest
paragraphs: ViewDeals started keeping its own record of TV prices at Walmart, Target and Best Buy on November 26, 2026. It is too short to prove anything yet, so everything above rests on the two sources named. As our record grows through a full year, we will add what our own checks show and say so here, including anywhere they disagree with the usual advice.
